name: Company Wide AI Rollouts
blurb: How drugmakers moved generative AI from pilots to the whole workforce.
title: Company Wide AI Rollouts
answer: Several large drugmakers have put generative AI in front of most employees. Moderna deployed ChatGPT Enterprise with a goal of proficiency for every eligible employee and a network of internal champions, and Amgen scaled AI assistants across the company after measured testing and security review.

crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Company wide AI rollouts in life sciences succeed on training, champions and clear policy, not on access alone.

Two large drugmakers show the pattern. Moderna deployed ChatGPT Enterprise with a goal of proficiency for every eligible employee and a network of internal champions. Amgen scaled AI assistants across the company after measured testing and security review. Both put the tool in front of most of the workforce, and both built support around it rather than leaving employees to find their own uses.

The governance layer is what makes that breadth possible in a regulated company. Enterprise agreements typically exclude customer data from model training, and the contract terms are where that is confirmed. Security review preceded Amgen's scale up. For life sciences specifically, the constraint is not model capability but which data may be entered at all, given patient records, regulated filings and unpublished research.

The data covers two companies and two accounts, one from 2024 and one from 2025. It does not report adoption rates, productivity results, or cost, so it cannot show that broad access produced measurable returns. It also says nothing about compute or power, and nothing here should be read as evidence about either.

The two rollouts differ in sequence, and the sequence is the transferable part. Moderna set the proficiency goal and the champions network as the deployment, treating the tool and the support as one package. Amgen ran measured testing and security review first, then scaled. Both orders end in the same place, which suggests the ordering is a function of how much the company already trusts its own review process rather than a difference in strategy.

The governance terms do work that the training does not. An enterprise agreement that excludes customer data from model training removes the question of whether a given prompt is safe to type, and that removal is what lets a rollout reach most of the workforce. In a regulated company the binding constraint is the data classification policy sitting on top of the contract, because patient records, regulated filings and unpublished research are excluded regardless of what the vendor permits.

The support layer also functions as a sorting mechanism. Role based training, prompt libraries and champions surface which workflows are worth building purpose built solutions for, so the broad rollout doubles as a discovery pass. Access without that layer produces scattered use and no signal about where to invest next.

Does enterprise AI use our data for training?
Enterprise agreements typically exclude customer data from model training, and the contract terms are where that is confirmed. Confirm the terms in your own contract rather than assuming the default.

What makes a company wide AI rollout succeed?
Training tied to real tasks, internal champions, clear policies and executive ownership. The data shows both Moderna and Amgen built support around the tool rather than leaving employees to find their own uses.

Did broad access produce measurable returns at either company?
The data does not hold this. It reports no adoption rates, productivity results or cost for either rollout, so it cannot show that access translated into returns.

How long did each rollout take from pilot to full workforce?
The data does not hold this. It gives one account dated 2024 for Moderna and one dated 2025-08 for Amgen, with no start dates or durations.

Which data can employees enter into these tools?
The data does not name specific categories beyond the exclusions. It states that life sciences companies add their own policies covering patient data, regulated records and unpublished research.

Why did Amgen run security review before scaling while Moderna led with the proficiency goal?
The data does not explain the difference. It records that Amgen scaled after measured testing and security review, and that Moderna set a proficiency goal with a champions network, without saying why each chose its order.

sections.heading: What it means for a life sciences leader

siblings.name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company

explainer:
A company wide rollout gives most employees access to an enterprise AI assistant, usually under a contract that keeps company data out of the vendor's model training and adds security controls such as single sign-on and audit logs. Life sciences companies add their own policies on which data may be used, especially patient data, regulated records and unpublished research.

The rollouts that report results invest heavily around the tool: role based training, libraries of use cases and prompts, internal champions who help colleagues, and measurement of adoption and outcomes. Access without that support tends to produce scattered, shallow use. Rollouts also surface which workflows deserve deeper, purpose built solutions.

What a company wide rollout involves

Giving every employee an AI assistant sounds like a software purchase. In a life sciences company it is a change programme. Research, clinical, manufacturing, safety, commercial and legal staff each face different rules about what data they may put into a tool and what they may do with its output. A rollout therefore means one approved platform, a data classification that tells people what is allowed, role specific guidance, and monitoring that shows how the tools are actually used.

The pattern that has worked

Companies that report success describe the same sequence. A secure enterprise version of a model, so that nothing typed in leaves the company's control. A short, mandatory introduction on rules and limits. A set of approved use cases for each function, with examples, and a route to propose new ones. Champions in each team who collect what works. And a steady stream of internal stories about time saved, which drives adoption more than any mandate. The least successful rollouts handed out licences and waited.

Measuring the result

Usage counts are the weakest measure, because they rise anyway. Better measures are hours saved on named tasks, the number of use cases that moved from pilot to routine, reductions in unapproved tool use, and the absence of incidents involving confidential data. Companies also watch for a two speed workforce, where some teams transform their work and others do not, because that gap becomes a management problem within a year.
